answers.text: Always give back three lines - delivery date, item and quantity, any change from the original order - same order every time, with consistent labels. If there's no change mentioned, write 'no change' instead of skipping it.
List each claim on its own line with date, amount, category and submitter, then total the amount column at the bottom so the total is worked out the same way every time.
The dates don't add up - the call was on the 14th, and the email says the 19th is three days out, but that's actually five days later.
The 15% increase in deliveries is right. But the on-time rate is off - 3 late out of 62 works out to about 95%, not 97%.
Output 2 - it shows the €612,000 and €25,100 behind the 4.1%. Output 1 could be right, but there's no way to check it without rerunning the numbers.
Reply 2, since it has the order and credit references to check. Reply 1's 'entirely our error' can't be verified as it is, though it's not necessarily wrong.
1. No, personal. 2. Yes, aggregate. 3. No, not released. 4. Yes, public. 5. No, personal.
The pricing and discount terms are sensitive enough that I'd hold those back, and the confidentiality clause naming both sides makes me want to be careful with the whole document.
Before the weekly report goes out, I cross-check the totals against the source system, which would catch a wrong number, not just a typo.
Step 4 is where a mistake becomes permanent since it sends automatically. Step 1 is worth watching too, since a bad read of the order feeds into everything after it.
